metadata.note: Wiscasset and Quebec Railroad (1895-1901) and its successor the Wiscasset, Waterville and Farmington (1901-1933): a 2 ft gauge steam common carrier from Wiscasset on the Sheepscot to Albion, with a branch from Weeks Mills Junction to Winslow (1902-1909 for passengers). The main line is split at the 12 Jun 1901 consolidation into two features sharing identical geometry, one per company (Rule 4). The 1907 receivership/reorganisation (Railroad Co. -> Railway Co.), the Peck era and Frank Winter's 1930 purchase are ownership changes under the same advertised name and are not split. It never reached Waterville, Farmington or Quebec.
metadata.freight_only_audit: Nothing drawn after passenger service ended. Not drawn: Weeks Mills - North Vassalboro freight Apr 1909 - c.1916 and North Vassalboro - Winslow freight Apr 1909 - 1912 (Winslow Branch drawn 1902-1909 only); the Wiscasset transfer yard and wharf on pilings, MEC interchange, and the industrial spurs along the line; the never-operated Albion - Burnham Junction extension grade; the Jun - Oct 1933 mail truck (road, not rail).
metadata.horsecar_audit: None. Steam from the first train, 20 Feb 1895.
not_yet_sourced: Passengers 1925-1933 on Wiscasset - Albion (wwf-wiscasset-albion): 1933 is the end of ALL rail operation (15 Jun 1933 derailment), and the regular train of the early 1930s was a mixed train carrying the RPO/mail, but no source found names passengers after Fowler's 1924 public timetable. Moody, 'The Maine Two-Footers', or the Jones/Crittenden WW&F histories would settle it. If required, the conservative confirmed end is 1924.
No Wiscasset and Quebec timetable was found; headway_min for 1895-1901 is carried back from the 1902/1909 WW&F pattern.
Whether trains of Jul 1901 - Jun 1902 were advertised under the W&Q or the WW&F name, and whether Wiscasset - Albion service had any gap in 1901-02, is unverified; neither changes a drawn year.
Possible special passenger trains on the Winslow Branch after Apr 1909 ('may be advertised on special dates') - none found; not drawn.
Peck's purchase date: The Town Line says 1906, the museum history 1907. Not a split either way.
Exact sites of the Wiscasset and Winslow stations are not pinned; each line ends at the end of the mapped grade (see geometry_quality).
avg_speed_kmh and all headway_min values are estimates; no running times were read.

properties.geometry_quality: Fully traced on the road's own OSM-mapped 2 ft grade; no straight-line legs. Traced 43.3 mi (69.7 km) against 43.5 mi documented (Fowler, Maine lines 46-47: Wiscasset 0.0, Weeks Mills 28.2, Albion 28.2+15.3; Wikipedia MP 43.5). By leg: Wiscasset - Weeks Mills Junction 28.5 mi traced vs 28.2 documented; Weeks Mills Junction - Albion 14.9 mi traced vs 15.3 documented. South end: the last OSM WW&F vertex (43.99945,-69.66530), ~30 m short of the Maine Central Rockland Branch (knox_and_lincoln_railway.geojson) at the WW&F/MEC diamond beside which the WW&F station stood; the line is not drawn onto MEC track, nor out onto the transfer wharf (freight). The exact station building site is not pinned. North end: the end of OSM way 531868364 at the Albion depot area (44.53713,-69.44530). EXCLUDED: the WW&F-named ways north of Albion (1350733504, 1350733505, 676786504), which are the never-operated Albion - Burnham Junction extension grade; the short Albion yard/preserved ways 676786500, 676786501, 676786503, 183382263; and the WW&F Railway Museum's sidings in Alna (335283054, 992225883), which are a modern tourist operation, not this road. Era: the grade drawn is the road's own 1895-1933 alignment (rail lifted 1934); no later alignment. About 3.4 mi in Alna runs over the museum's rebuilt track, which is relaid on the original grade.

segments.note: Wiscasset and Quebec Railroad, 2 ft gauge steam common carrier. Construction began Jun 1894; operations to Weeks Mills (28 mi from Wiscasset) began 20 Feb 1895, and Albion, 44 mi out and 'the end of the first leg to Quebec', was reached in Nov 1895 (WW&F Railway Museum history; The Town Line; Wikipedia). Both legs opened within 1895, so at year resolution the whole line starts in 1895; the Wiscasset - Weeks Mills section ran alone Feb - Nov 1895. Steam from the first train - no animal-power era. Jackson & Sharp built four passenger cars for the opening (Wikipedia). Alna appears in the 1900 Pathfinder Guide (Fowler, Maine line 46, 'Alna 1900PG'), a dated public passenger listing. Ends in 1901 because the W&Q was consolidated into the Wiscasset, Waterville and Farmington on 12 Jun 1901 (Portland Daily Press, 13 Jun 1901); the trains continue under the new company in the next feature. Receivers ran the road in its later W&Q years under the W&Q name. headway_min is an ESTIMATE: no W&Q timetable was found; ~480 min (two trains each way a day) is carried back from the 1902/1909 WW&F pattern and is not sourced for 1895-1901.
sources: Segment-level: opening dates from the WW&F Railway Museum history, The Town Line and Wikipedia (which agree); 1900 passenger listing from Fowler's Maine stations list (Pathfinder Guide, 'Alna 1900PG'); end at the 12 Jun 1901 consolidation from the Portland Daily Press, 13 Jun 1901, p1. headway_min is an estimate, not sourced for these years.

segments.note: Wiscasset, Waterville and Farmington Railroad Co., formed by the consolidation of the Wiscasset and Quebec, the Waterville and Weeks Mills and the Franklin, Somerset and Kennebec, stock transferred at Waterville 12 Jun 1901 (Portland Daily Press, 13 Jun 1901). From 16 Jun 1902 the through trains ran Wiscasset - Winslow over the new Winslow Branch and Albion was served by a shuttle from Weeks Mills Junction: the Jan 1909 public timetable (Daily Kennebec Journal, Feb-Mar 1909) shows two Weeks Mills Jct - Albion round trips a day. Every main-line and Albion-line stop is in the company's 1902 public timetable (Fowler, 'a'). Receivership 1907, auction, reorganised as the Wiscasset, Waterville and Farmington Railway Co. under Carson Peck (museum history gives 1907; The Town Line gives Peck's purchase as 1906) - same road, same name to the passenger, not a change of operator. Whether trains in Jul 1901 - Jun 1902 were still advertised under the W&Q name is not known; the split year is the corporate act. headway_min is an ESTIMATE from the Jan 1909 timetable (two trains each way on the Albion line), not a schedule for every year.
sources: Segment-level: consolidation from the Portland Daily Press, 13 Jun 1901, p1; Jun 1902 through service from the Daily Kennebec Journal, 16 Jun 1902, p8; Jan 1909 timetable from the Daily Kennebec Journal, 24 Feb 1909, p3; 1902 public timetable from Fowler's Maine list ('a'); 1907 receivership from the WW&F Railway Museum history. headway_min is an estimate.

segments.note: After passenger service on the Winslow Branch was cancelled in Apr 1909 (Daily Kennebec Journal, 22 Apr 1909), Wiscasset - Albion was again the through main line: a Waterville - China stage was ordered in Jul 1909 'to connect with the morning train from Albion to Wiscasset' (Daily Kennebec Journal, 7 Jul 1909). 'By 1913 ... daily freight and passenger service 43.5 miles north to Albion' (Wikipedia, Wiscasset, Maine - uncited there). The road carried 13,291 passengers in 1915 (Maine PUC report, Daily Kennebec Journal, 17 Mar 1916). Every main-line and Albion-line stop is in the company's 1924 public timetable (Fowler, 'b'). Peck died 1915; his heirs held it until the 1930 receivership, when Frank Winter bought it for $6,000 and ran it under the WW&F name to the end - ownership only, not a change of operator. The Wiscasset enginehouse fire of 1931 destroyed engines 6 and 7, replaced by ex-Kennebec Central 8 and 9. END YEAR: 1933 is the end of ALL rail operation - on 15 Jun 1933 the morning train down from Albion derailed in Whitefield and operations ceased (WW&F Railway Museum, Wikipedia, The Town Line agree); mail went by truck until Oct 1933, which is road, not rail, and is not drawn. In the early 1930s the regular train was the morning Albion - Wiscasset train and afternoon return, a mixed train carrying the railway post office (the last 2 ft gauge RPO in the US). No source found names PASSENGERS after Fowler's 1924 timetable; carriage of passengers in 1925-1933 rests on secondary descriptions of that regular mixed/mail train. If a source naming passengers is required, the conservative confirmed end is 1924. headway_min is an ESTIMATE (two trains each way a day per the 1909 timetable and the early-1930s two-train pattern), not a schedule for every year.
sources: Segment-level: Apr 1909 through-line change from the Daily Kennebec Journal, 22 Apr and 7 Jul 1909, p3; 1915 passenger count from the Daily Kennebec Journal, 17 Mar 1916, p11; 1924 public timetable from Fowler's Maine list ('b'); 15 Jun 1933 end from the WW&F Railway Museum history, Wikipedia and The Town Line. Passengers in 1925-1933 are NOT confirmed by any source naming them (see metadata.not_yet_sourced). headway_min is an estimate.

properties.line: Wiscasset, Waterville and Farmington: Winslow Branch
properties.speed_source: ESTIMATE: no running time was read from a timetable. ~22 km/h assumes about three hours for the 43.5 mi Wiscasset - Albion run on a 2 ft gauge steam road with mixed-train work, in line with the other Maine two-footers in this dataset.
properties.geometry_source: OpenStreetMap way 183381350 (railway=abandoned, gauge=610, name 'Wiscasset, Waterville and Farmington Railway'), fetched 2026-10-14 from the mail.ru Overpass mirror; it shares OSM node 1937516325 with the main line at Weeks Mills Junction. Douglas-Peucker 8 m + trim_reversals (opstrace.py). Cross-checked against OpenHistoricalMap way 201885362 ('Wiscasset, Waterville and Farmington Railway', 1901-1933, USGS 3DEP lidar-named), which follows the same grade within ~100 m for most of its length (max 320 m, where OHM's coarser vertices cut corners near China Lake / East Vassalboro) and is 13.9 mi long.
properties.geometry_quality: Fully traced on one OSM abandoned-grade way; no straight-line legs. Traced 13.8 mi (22.2 km) against 14.5 mi documented (Fowler / Wikipedia: Winslow MP 42.7 less Weeks Mills MP 28.2) - about 5% short; the main-line trace puts the junction 0.3 mi further from Wiscasset than Fowler's 28.2, which accounts for part of the difference. Winslow end: the end of OSM way 183381350 (44.53280,-69.63669), on the east bank of the Kennebec about 0.3 mi from the river's centreline; OHM's grade ends ~240 m further north-east (44.53410,-69.63424). Neither marks the Winslow station building, whose exact site is not pinned; the line is NOT carried across the Kennebec - the WW&F never reached Waterville. An untagged abandoned OSM way (179905399) continuing north-east along the Winslow riverbank was NOT used: nothing ties it to the WW&F. Era: the grade drawn is the branch's own 1902-c.1916 alignment (Winslow end lifted 1912); no later alignment.

segments.note: Winslow Branch, built as the Waterville and Weeks Mills RR (consolidated into the WW&F Jun 1901) to reach Waterville; it stopped at Winslow on the east bank of the Kennebec, with a transfer bus from City Hall Square, Waterville. Most of the grade was finished in 1898-99 (The Town Line), but no passenger train is known before 16 Jun 1902, when 'a temporary train service between Winslow and Wiscasset' began, with the full summer schedule from 23 Jun 1902 (Daily Kennebec Journal, 16 Jun 1902). All branch stops (South China, China Lake, Clark's, East Vassalboro, North Vassalboro, Winslow) are in the company's 1902 public timetable and none in its 1924 one (Fowler, 'a' only). Jan 1909 timetable: Winslow 6.20 AM to Wiscasset daily and 10.15 AM Wed & Sat; Winslow - Weeks Mills Jct 4.25 PM; northbound 7.30 AM Weeks Mills Jct - Winslow, 9.30 AM (Wed & Sat) and 3.40 PM from Wiscasset (Daily Kennebec Journal, Feb-Mar 1909). Ends 1909: passenger service Winslow - Weeks Mills 'cancelled - freight accepted', reported from Waterville 21 Apr 1909 (Daily Kennebec Journal, 22 Apr 1909), confirmed by the Jul 1909 report of the 'discontinuance' of the road between Weeks' Mills and Waterville. The headline allowed that trains 'may be advertised on special dates for passengers'; no such special was found, so none is drawn. Freight continued: the Winslow end's rails were lifted in 1912, freight ran to North Vassalboro a few more years (Wikipedia dates the branch 1902-1916), and the remains were scrapped by the mid-1920s - none of that carried passengers and none is drawn. headway_min (~420 min, two to three trains each way a day) is an ESTIMATE from the Jan 1909 timetable.
sources: Segment-level: opening from the Daily Kennebec Journal, 16 Jun 1902, p8; Jan 1909 timetable from the Daily Kennebec Journal, 24 Feb 1909, p3; passenger end from the Daily Kennebec Journal, 22 Apr 1909 and 7 Jul 1909, p3; branch stops in the 1902 timetable only per Fowler's Maine list. headway_min is an estimate.
